title: Where is thy sting (1 Corinthians 15:51–57)
hook: O death, where is thy victory

segments.voice: Yesterday, enigma: a dim bronze mirror seen in a dark manner, and the hope of seeing face to face. Your line was then, face to face. What did you leave unanswered? Day five hundred seventy-six.

Some people in Corinth had decided the dead don't rise. Souls might go on, they thought, but bodies? Bodies rot. Paul answers them in chapter fifteen, and it's an argument most of the way through. He reasons, he lists the people who saw the risen Christ, he talks about seeds and harvest. And then, near the end, the argument turns into something more like a song. He starts taunting death itself, as if it were a bully that's finally been beaten.
screen: `SOME SAY THE DEAD DON'T RISE.` → `PAUL ANSWERS IN CHAPTER FIFTEEN.` → `AN ARGUMENT TURNS INTO A SONG.`

segments.voice: He begins with a secret: "Behold, I tell you a mystery." Then the Douay-Rheims, following the Latin Vulgate, reads: "We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed." Bibles translated from the Greek put it the other way round: we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed. The copies of the letter differ here, and translators follow the text they have. Either way, Paul's point stands: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet, the dead will rise incorruptible. Then he borrows from the prophet Hosea and makes it a dare: "O death, where is thy victory? O death, where is thy sting?" The Greek word for sting is kentron. It's the stinger of a bee or a scorpion, and also the goad a farmer used to drive an ox. Paul names the stinger in the next breath: the sting of death is sin. Preachers sometimes add a picture: a bee that stings once leaves its stinger behind. In that picture, death stung Christ, and lost its sting. And Paul doesn't end with a final argument. He ends with thanks: "But thanks be to God, who hath given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ." Catholics hear this chapter at funerals and confess it every Sunday in the Creed: I look forward to the resurrection of the dead. The Church never pretends death doesn't hurt. A few verses earlier, Paul himself calls death an enemy, the last one to be destroyed. An enemy, he says, but a beaten one.
screen: `A MYSTERY: WE SHALL BE CHANGED.` · `TWO READINGS OF ONE VERSE.` · `KENTRON: THE STINGER, THE GOAD.` · `THANKS BE TO GOD: THE VICTORY.` · then, large: `O DEATH, WHERE IS THY STING?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone near the end. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is dying, or very old, or very sick. Someone you know, or someone you've only heard about, or the people in a hospital you pass on the way to work. If that's too close today, think of everyone in the world who will die tonight. Picture them with care. If you pray, you can pray for them in your own words, or pray the Hail Mary, which asks Mary to pray for us now and at the hour of our death. If you don't, hold them in mind and wish them peace. The bell holds the time.
Kentron. The Greek word for a stinger or an ox-goad: Paul's taunt at death, whose sting, sin, Christ has drawn. Today's word.
Your line: death, where is thy sting. Today, when you hear of a death, near or far, say the line quietly, and think of the person, not just the news. Day five hundred seventy-six.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the dying, and the Church offers the anointing of the sick and Viaticum, a last Communion; 1 Corinthians 15 is among the readings for a Catholic funeral.

fork.setup: some in Corinth say the dead don't rise. you're Paul, at the end of a long argument. how do you finish?
options: concede that only souls go on.
taunt death, and give thanks for the victory.
say it doesn't matter either way.
fork.reveal: "O death, where is thy sting?" then: "thanks be to God, who hath given us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ."

original.note: Greek: a sting, or an ox-goad. 'the sting of death is sin' (1 Corinthians 15:56).

trapdoor: what you thought: a brave saying for funerals.
what it means: Paul taunts death because Christ is risen, and the dead will rise changed.
what a scholar hears: kentron, the goad and the stinger; Hosea 13:14 reworked; and a famous variant reading in 15:51 between Greek and Latin copies.

notes: 1 Corinthians 15 (58 verses) as the letter's longest chapter. Confirm.
Variant at 15:51: the Vulgate reading ('omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur') vs. the majority Greek reading. Stated neutrally; confirm the Douay-Rheims wording.
The bee-stinger image is described as a preachers' illustration, not as the meaning of the text.
Creed wording 'I look forward to the resurrection of the dead' is the current English Missal; paraphrased, not cited as a quotation. Confirm.
Practice is about someone near death; gentle alternative offered for listeners in fresh grief.
